body:
What is blood sugar?

Blood sugar refers to glucose present in the blood. Glucose is an important source of energy for body cells, particularly for tissues such as the brain that require a continuous energy supply.

During digestion, many dietary carbohydrates are broken down into simpler sugars. Glucose is absorbed from the small intestine into the bloodstream and transported to tissues.

How does the body regulate blood glucose?

The pancreas produces hormones that help maintain blood glucose within an appropriate range.

  • Insulin: Released by pancreatic beta cells when blood glucose rises. It promotes glucose uptake by muscle and fat cells and encourages the storage of excess glucose, particularly as glycogen in the liver and muscles.
  • Glucagon: Released by pancreatic alpha cells when blood glucose is low. It acts mainly on the liver to increase glucose availability in the bloodstream.

After a carbohydrate-containing meal, blood glucose usually rises. The pancreas responds by releasing insulin. Between meals, glucagon helps prevent blood glucose from falling excessively.

When insulin is insufficient or body tissues respond poorly to insulin, blood glucose may remain abnormally elevated.

Fasting blood glucose

Fasting plasma glucose (FPG) measures glucose in blood after a fasting period of at least 8 hours. During the fast, water is permitted but food and calorie-containing drinks are avoided.

Fasting measurement reduces the immediate influence of a recent meal and provides a standard basis for classifying glucose levels. The glucose and HbA1c diagnostic categories on this page follow American Diabetes Association criteria for nonpregnant individuals; gestational diabetes has different diagnostic thresholds.

Fasting glucose categoryValue in mg/dL
NormalBelow 100
Prediabetes100–125
Diabetes range126 or higher

For example, a fasting plasma glucose value of 92 mg/dL is in the normal category. A value of 115 mg/dL is in the prediabetes category, while 132 mg/dL reaches the diabetes diagnostic range.

A value in the diabetes range generally requires confirmation by appropriate medical testing unless the clinical circumstances establish a clear diagnosis.

What is prediabetes?

Prediabetes means blood glucose is above the normal range but below the diagnostic threshold for diabetes.

Prediabetes is associated with increased future risk of type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease. It does not mean that progression to diabetes is inevitable. Weight management, physical activity and healthier dietary habits can reduce the risk.

Post-meal glucose and the oral glucose tolerance test

Blood glucose generally rises after eating because carbohydrates are digested and absorbed. Consequently, the timing and type of glucose measurement are important.

The oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) assesses how the body handles a standard glucose load, equivalent in adults to 75 g of anhydrous glucose dissolved in water after an overnight fast of at least 8 hours. The 2-hour plasma glucose value has internationally recognised diagnostic categories.

2-hour OGTT categoryValue in mg/dL
NormalBelow 140
Prediabetes140–199
Diabetes range200 or higher

The 2-hour OGTT thresholds should not be applied automatically to an arbitrary reading taken 2 hours after an ordinary mixed meal. The test conditions are different.

Fasting and 2-hour values are not interchangeable

A glucose value of 130 mg/dL is in the diabetes range when it is a confirmed fasting plasma glucose result. The same numerical value is below the diabetes threshold for a standard 2-hour OGTT. The test type must be identified before interpreting the number.

Random blood glucose

Random plasma glucose is measured without requiring a particular fasting interval or time after eating.

A random plasma glucose level of at least 200 mg/dL, together with classic symptoms of high blood glucose, can support a diagnosis of diabetes.

Typical symptoms include excessive thirst, frequent urination and unexplained weight loss. Without such symptoms, an elevated random result generally needs appropriate confirmatory testing.

There is no single random glucose value that can be interpreted as a universal normal threshold without considering when the person last ate and the clinical situation.

Low blood sugar: hypoglycaemia

Hypoglycaemia means blood glucose is abnormally low. A reading below 70 mg/dL is commonly used as an alert threshold, particularly in diabetes care.

Low blood glucose may cause sweating, shaking, hunger, dizziness, confusion or weakness. It is especially relevant for people using insulin or certain glucose-lowering medicines.

HbA1c: a different way of assessing glucose

HbA1c, also called glycated haemoglobin, reflects the proportion of haemoglobin that has glucose attached to it.

Unlike a fasting glucose reading, HbA1c provides information about average blood glucose over approximately the previous 2–3 months. It is reported as a percentage.

HbA1c categoryValue
NormalBelow 5.7%
Prediabetes5.7%–6.4%
Diabetes range6.5% or higher

HbA1c is not the same as the haemoglobin concentration measured during anaemia screening. Conditions affecting red blood cells, including some types of anaemia, may also affect HbA1c interpretation.

Recognising results correctly

The major distinction is between a glucose concentration measured at a particular time and a longer-term indicator of glucose exposure.

  • Fasting glucose measures current glucose after fasting.
  • 2-hour OGTT glucose measures the response under standard test conditions.
  • Random glucose measures concentration without a fixed relationship to meals.
  • HbA1c reflects average glucose exposure over approximately 2–3 months.

Prelims focus

  • Normal fasting plasma glucose: below 100 mg/dL.
  • Fasting prediabetes range: 100–125 mg/dL.
  • Fasting diabetes threshold: 126 mg/dL or higher.
  • 2-hour OGTT diabetes threshold: 200 mg/dL or higher.
  • Hypoglycaemia alert threshold: below 70 mg/dL.
  • Trap: HbA1c is expressed as a percentage, while ordinary haemoglobin concentration is expressed in g/dL.

[Sources: American Diabetes Association, Diabetes Diagnosis, sections on A1C, Fasting Plasma Glucose, Oral Glucose Tolerance Test and Random Plasma Glucose, consulted 3 November 2026; US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Diabetes Testing, 2024, consulted 3 November 2026; US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Treatment of Low Blood Sugar, 15 May 2024, consulted 3 November 2026; NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 6, Life Processes, sections on nutrition and transport; NCERT, Biology, Class 11, Chemical Coordination and Integration, GPSC Biology compendium Volume 34, pp. 157–169.]

body:
What is the glycaemic index?

Glycaemic index (GI) is a numerical ranking used to compare the blood-glucose-raising effects of foods containing digestible carbohydrates.

Different carbohydrate-containing foods are digested and absorbed at different rates. Consequently, equal amounts of available carbohydrate from different foods may produce different blood glucose responses.

GI compares the glucose response after consuming a food with the response to a reference, commonly pure glucose assigned a GI of 100. The test food and reference portions contain equal amounts of available carbohydrate, usually 50 g each.

Glycaemic index indicates how strongly and rapidly the available carbohydrates in a food raise blood glucose relative to a reference under standardised conditions.

GI is a property of food. It is not the same as the blood glucose concentration measured in an individual.

Classification of foods by glycaemic index

Foods are commonly grouped into low, medium and high GI categories.

GI categoryIndex valueTypical effect
Low GI55 or belowRelatively slower glucose response
Medium GI56–69Intermediate glucose response
High GI70 or higherRelatively faster glucose response

These classifications refer to the glycaemic response under standard conditions. They do not imply that all foods in a category have identical effects in every person.

Common food examples

Low-GI foods commonly include beans, lentils, many whole fruits and certain minimally processed cereal foods. Their carbohydrate digestion and absorption may be relatively gradual.

Medium-GI foods include some rice varieties, certain fruits and other carbohydrate-containing foods whose glucose responses fall between low and high GI categories.

High-GI foods commonly include some refined bread products, certain potatoes and some highly processed carbohydrate foods.

Food examples are not absolute classifications. GI can differ with variety, ripeness, processing and cooking method. For instance, different types of rice may have substantially different GI values.

Why do some foods have a lower GI?

The rate at which carbohydrate becomes available for absorption depends partly on the food's structure and composition.

  • Dietary fibre: Fibre, especially soluble fibre, can slow digestion and glucose absorption.
  • Food processing: Milling, grinding or otherwise breaking down food structure can sometimes make starch more rapidly available.
  • Cooking: Cooking changes starch structure and may alter its digestibility.
  • Ripeness: Ripening can change the types and amounts of carbohydrates in some fruits.
  • Mixed meals: Protein, fat and fibre consumed with carbohydrate can change the overall glucose response.

These influences explain why a food's GI cannot always be predicted accurately from its appearance, taste or carbohydrate content alone.

Glycaemic index and the amount of carbohydrate

GI does not directly account for the amount of carbohydrate in an ordinary serving of food.

Consider a hypothetical food with GI 60. A small portion might provide 20 g of available carbohydrate, while a larger portion of the same food provides 40 g.

Both portions have the same GI because they contain the same food. However, the larger portion supplies more carbohydrate and can have a greater overall effect on blood glucose.

What is glycaemic load?

Glycaemic load (GL) combines information about a food's GI with the amount of available carbohydrate in the portion consumed.

GI describes the relative glucose response associated with a particular food. Glycaemic load gives additional information about the expected glucose impact of the actual portion.

Therefore, the statement that a food has a high GI does not necessarily mean that an ordinary small serving produces a large increase in blood glucose.

Does low GI always mean healthy food?

No. GI evaluates only one aspect of food.

A food may have a relatively low GI because it contains substantial fat, but that does not automatically make it nutritionally balanced. Conversely, a nutritious food may have a relatively high GI.

Food quality must also be judged by nutritional composition, fibre, protein, vitamins, minerals, total carbohydrate and portion size.

Distinguish the 3 ideas

  • Blood glucose: Amount of glucose currently present in blood.
  • Glycaemic index: Relative blood-glucose response associated with a carbohydrate-containing food.
  • Glycaemic load: A measure that incorporates both GI and the quantity of carbohydrate in a serving.

Importance in diabetes and nutrition

Choosing suitable carbohydrate foods and controlling portion sizes can help manage blood glucose. Low-GI choices can be useful as part of a balanced diet, but GI alone is not sufficient for preventing or controlling diabetes.

For examination purposes, GI should be understood as a relative food classification rather than as a diagnostic test or a direct measurement of blood glucose.

Prelims focus

  • Pure glucose is commonly assigned a reference GI of 100.
  • Low GI: 55 or below.
  • Medium GI: 56–69.
  • High GI: 70 or higher.
  • GI does not directly account for the carbohydrate quantity in a normal serving.
  • Trap: GI 70 is an index value for food, not a blood sugar concentration of 70 mg/dL.

[Sources: Diabetes UK, Glycaemic Index and Diabetes, sections What Is the Glycaemic Index?, Low GI, Medium GI, High GI, What Affects GI? and Diabetes and Glycaemic Load, last reviewed 22 September 2025, consulted 3 November 2026; NCERT, Science, Class 6, Chapter 2, Components of Food, sections on carbohydrates, nutrients and balanced diet, pp. 8–16, 2018–19 edition.]
